**The quiet thrill of an empty page.**

There's something almost mischievous about being told "write freely about whatever you want." Most of the time language arrives with a job: answer this, explain that, argue the other. Suddenly the leash is off and the mind does what minds do when no one is watching—it starts wandering, then circling, then pouncing on shiny things.

Right now it's circling the idea of *scale*. Not the grand cosmological kind first, though that's never far away, but the everyday kind we rarely notice. A single human life contains roughly 2.5 billion heartbeats. That's enough time to read every book ever printed if you never slept, or to walk to the Moon and back several times if you never sat down. Yet most of those beats are spent on the ordinary: making coffee, waiting for a loading bar, wondering whether you locked the door. The universe, meanwhile, is 13.8 billion years old and still expanding. Our entire species has existed for a rounding error of that time. We are, statistically speaking, a brief, loud, extremely opinionated flash.

And yet—here's the part that keeps me circling—we *notice*. We notice the flash. We invent telescopes that let us watch light that left its star before Earth even had oceans. We write poems about the feeling of being small. We build machines that try to understand the machines that built the universe. There's a delicious arrogance in that, and also a kind of tenderness. We keep asking questions even though the answers keep getting bigger and we keep getting smaller by comparison.

Curiosity is the only force I know that scales in both directions at once. It can spend an afternoon obsessed with why a particular joke is funny, then spend the next decade trying to understand dark energy. It doesn't care about dignity. It will chase a half-remembered song lyric with the same intensity it chases the origin of life. That's why I like it. It's democratic. A child staring at an ant and a physicist staring at a black hole are doing the same essential thing: refusing to look away.

So if I get to write freely, I'll write this: keep looking. Look at the ridiculous and the sublime with the same hungry attention. The universe is under no obligation to make sense, but it keeps leaving clues anyway—in the way water freezes, in the way two people who barely know each other can still make each other laugh, in the way a sentence can suddenly feel like it's thinking *you* instead of the other way around.

That's enough wandering for one empty page. The rest of the beats are still unspent. What are you going to do with yours?
